feedback.problem: Given that $y=y(t)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+64y=0,$ which of the following is **not** a solution to this equation?
feedback.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda t}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda t},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda t}+64{e}^{\lambda t} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda t}({\lambda }^{2}+64) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
{\lambda }^{2}+64=0.
$$

Solving the auxiliary equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+64 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-64 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 8\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\lambda =\pm 8\text{i}$ are the (purely imaginary) roots of the auxiliary equation. 

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions $\text{Re}({e}^{8\text{i}t})=\operatorname{cos}⁡8t$ and $\text{Im}({e}^{8\text{i}t})=\operatorname{sin}⁡8t$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only $\operatorname{sin}⁡8t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡4t$ is not a solution.
